author: Plato
biz: Run the Ring of Gyges Audit

Glaucon's challenge is really a compliance test. This week pull ten recorded calls and ten WhatsApp threads at random across HomeownersLoan and Apply4Loan, and read each as though the customer's daughter and your FCA file reviewer were both reading it. Add two questions to the quality sheet. Could this customer repeat back that you are a credit broker and not a lender, and could they repeat back what the loan costs and that their home is at risk. Measure the share passing both, broken down by adviser, and review it weekly rather than quarterly.
Let Each Part Do Its Own Work

Justice in Plato is each part doing its own work and not reaching for another's. Look for where that is breached at Debt Support Direct: whoever gains from a referral should not be the person judging whether a client is vulnerable or whether a solution is suitable. This week write down who owns the suitability decision, and make sure that role has no stake in the outcome, with a documented second check on every case flagged for vulnerability. Measure the proportion of cases carrying a recorded vulnerability check, and the proportion of those escalated.

b: Plato was born in Athens at about 428 BC, into a family that assumed it would one day run the place. His father Ariston was said to descend from the old kings of Attica, and his mother Perictione came from the line of Solon, who gave Athens its first serious laws. Her brother Charmides and her kinsman Critias were names any Athenian knew. In such a house politics was not a career you chose; it was what the men of the family did.

He was also born into a war. Athens and Sparta began fighting in 431 BC and did not stop until 404. In the second summer, plague came into the overcrowded city and killed perhaps a quarter of its people, Pericles among them in 429. Plato was a small child while Athens learned to live with mass funerals.

Then came the disasters his generation never forgot. In 415 the assembly voted to send a great fleet to conquer Sicily, and by 413 the fleet and the army were gone, dead or dying in the stone quarries of Syracuse. In 406, having just won a sea battle at Arginusae, the assembly tried its own victorious generals and executed several of them. In 404 Athens surrendered, and the long walls came down to the sound of flutes.
It matters that Plato did not learn in a classroom that a majority can be wrong. He learned it in a beaten city, among people who had voted with real enthusiasm for their own ruin.
ch.cap: An Athenian boy grows up inside a long war
ch.h: A Boy Born Into a Losing War

b: When the war ended, Sparta installed a government of thirty men to run Athens. Among them were Critias, Plato's kinsman, and Charmides, his uncle. Plato was in his early twenties. The door to power had swung open and the men inside it were family.

In the letter that comes down to us as his seventh, Plato says he was invited in and expected great things, because he imagined these men would lead the city out of an unjust life into a just one. What followed was eight months of killing. By the usual ancient estimate the Thirty put some fifteen hundred people to death and took their property, much of it from wealthy foreign residents whose money they wanted.

The episode that stayed with him was small. The Thirty sent for an elderly man named Socrates and ordered him to join a squad arresting Leon of Salamis, a rich man they meant to kill for his estate. Socrates listened to the order and went home. He said later, at his own trial, that he was not frightened of the government, only of doing something unjust.

So Plato watched two things at once. Men of his own class, holding absolute power and talking fluently about virtue, turned out to be thieves and murderers. An awkward stonemason's son with no office and no protection simply declined. Within the year the Thirty were finished, Critias dead in the fighting at Munychia, and the democracy was back. Plato withdrew from public life in disgust.
ch.cap: The Thirty rule Athens and one old man refuses
ch.h: Thirty Men and One Stubborn Teacher

b: Four years later the restored democracy did something Plato found worse than anything the Thirty managed. In 399 BC Socrates, then about seventy, was prosecuted for impiety and for corrupting the young. A jury of several hundred ordinary Athenians found him guilty by a modest margin, and then, when he refused to plead for mercy, sentenced him to death.

Plato was about twenty eight. In the Apology he names himself among the friends at the trial who offered to pay a fine instead. In the Phaedo, which describes the last day in the cell, the narrator notes that Plato was not there, he thinks through illness. Either way the point is the same. The wisest man in Athens was killed by a show of hands, lawfully, by ordinary citizens following a fair procedure to its end.

Here is the question the rest of his life answers. If the many can vote to invade Sicily, and vote to kill their own winning generals, and vote to execute Socrates, then what exactly is justice, and who could be trusted to do it? Not what Athenians happen to call just. Not what the law of the moment permits. What is it in itself, when nobody is voting.
That is where The Republic begins, and it is not an academic exercise. It is a man trying to understand how the best city he knew came to kill the best man he knew.
ch.cap: A jury of citizens sentences Socrates to death

b: After the execution, Plato and other followers of Socrates left Athens and went up the coast to Megara, where another of the circle kept a school. Later writers send him on to Egypt and Cyrene, but those journeys are thinly evidenced and may be invention.

One voyage is better attested. At around 388 BC, in his late thirties, he sailed west to southern Italy and Sicily. In Tarentum he met Archytas, a mathematician and engineer of the Pythagorean tradition who also governed the city, a man who did geometry in the morning and ran a state in the afternoon.

Mathematics did something to Plato that argument alone had not. In geometry he met truths no assembly could overturn. The square on the hypotenuse does not shrink because a crowd is angry, and the ratio of a circle to its diameter cannot be sent into exile by a vote. If there were knowledge like that about justice, then the jury that killed Socrates had not merely been cruel. It had been wrong, in the flat way a man is wrong about a sum.

On the same journey he reached Syracuse, the richest Greek city in the west, ruled by Dionysius the first, a tyrant with a large fleet and a thin skin. There Plato made a friend for life in Dion, the tyrant's young brother in law. A famous story says Dionysius grew so irritated by his conversation that he had him sold in the slave market on Aegina, until a man from Cyrene bought his freedom. The tale is old but doubtful.
ch.cap: Plato sails west and finds mathematics
ch.h: Geometry and a Tyrant in the West
ch.when: Megara, Italy and Syracuse, 399 to 388 BC

b: Back in Athens at around 387 BC, Plato acquired ground near a grove sacred to a hero called Academus, about a mile beyond the city wall, and began to teach. We call what grew out of it the Academy. It was less a university than a permanent community doing mathematics, astronomy, law and argument together, and it lasted in some form for close to three centuries, until a Roman siege wrecked that suburb in 86 BC.

A late tradition says the words let no one ignorant of geometry enter were carved over the door. There is no good early evidence for it, but it catches the place. In 367 BC a seventeen year old arrived from the north to study there and stayed twenty years. His name was Aristotle.

Somewhere in these years, most likely in the 370s, he wrote the long dialogue in ten parts we call The Republic. Its Greek title, Politeia, means something closer to the regime, the whole arrangement of a community. Plato puts himself nowhere in it. The speaker is Socrates, brought back to life on the page to go on asking the question that killing him had not settled.

He sets the scene with care. Socrates is walking up from the harbour at Piraeus after a festival when a group of young men more or less kidnap him for the evening. They end up in the house of a rich shield manufacturer. Two of the young men pressing him hardest, Glaucon and Adeimantus, were Plato's own brothers.
ch.cap: The Academy opens in a grove beyond the wall

b: The first answers are the ordinary ones, and Socrates takes them apart. Justice is telling the truth and paying your debts, says old Cephalus, until a case appears where handing a weapon back to a friend who has lost his mind would be madness. Justice is helping friends and harming enemies, says his son Polemarchus, until it turns out we are poor judges of who our friends are.

Then a professional arguer called Thrasymachus loses patience and says the thing the whole book exists to answer. Justice, he says, is nothing but the advantage of the stronger. Laws are written by whoever holds power, in their own interest, and taught to everybody else as morality. The just man is a sucker who ends up poorer than the unjust one, and the truly successful injustice is not burglary but tyranny, done wholesale with the city's blessing.

Socrates wins on points, and Plato is honest enough to show that this is not enough. Glaucon calls it a trick and demands a real answer. He tells of a shepherd named Gyges who finds a ring that makes him invisible, and who promptly seduces the queen, kills the king and takes the kingdom. Put that ring on the most upright man in Athens, Glaucon says, and watch what he does within a month. Then picture a perfectly unjust man with a flawless reputation beside a perfectly just man taken for a monster, and ask which life you would choose for your own son.
That is the real challenge. Not is justice useful, which everybody grants. Is justice good for the person who has it, stripped of reward, with no credit, even punished for it.
ch.cap: Glaucon asks why anyone would be just unseen
ch.h: The Ring That Makes You Invisible
ch.when: In the dialogue: Piraeus, one evening

b: Justice in a single person is small and hard to see, Socrates says, so let us build a city in words instead and watch justice appear in something large enough to read. The city grows from a village of farmers and shoemakers, each doing the one thing he does well, into something that needs soldiers who will not turn on the people they guard.

So much of the middle of the book is about education: what children are told, what music they hear, what they are taught to love before they are old enough for reasons. Plato will censor the poets for this, Homer included, because you cannot describe gods behaving badly to a child and expect the adult to behave well.

Out of this come three groups: the many who produce, the guards who protect, and the few who rule. And in the fourth book the answer arrives. Justice is not a particular action. It is each part doing its own work and not reaching for another's. A city is just when producers produce, soldiers defend and the wise decide.

Then he turns it inwards, which was the point all along. A soul has three parts: reason, a spirited part that feels indignation and shame, and an appetitive part that wants food and money and sex. A thirsty man sometimes refuses a drink, and one thing wanting one thing cannot explain that. He tells of Leontius, who passed the executioner's ground desperate to look at the corpses and furious with himself for wanting to.

So a just soul is one where reason governs, spirit enforces, and appetite is fed but not obeyed. Injustice is civil war in a single head, which answers Glaucon. It is not a profitable crime but a disease of the one thing you can never get away from.
ch.cap: A city is built in speech to make justice visible
ch.h: A City Built to See a Soul

b: Who could be trusted to run such a place? Plato's answer is the most famous and most disliked sentence in the book: until philosophers rule as kings, or those who now rule become genuine philosophers, there will be no end to trouble for cities or for the human race.

He means something precise by philosopher. A philosopher is not a clever talker but someone in love with what is actually the case rather than with how things look, trained for years in geometry, astronomy and dialectic, which means having your best arguments taken to pieces. Above it all Plato puts the Form of the Good, which is to the mind what the sun is to the eye. It does not merely let you see things. It is why there is anything to see.

Men sit chained in a cave facing a blank wall. Behind them a fire burns, and between the fire and their backs other men carry puppets, so shadows move across the wall. The shadows are simply what things are, because they have never seen anything else. Free one and the firelight hurts. Drag him up into daylight and he is blinded and angry and sure the shadows were clearer.

What people forget is the ending. The man who gets out does not stay out. He must go back down into the dark, where his eyes no longer work and he argues clumsily about shadows with men who never left, and where, Socrates says drily, they would kill him if they could. Plato wrote that twenty five years after a jury killed Socrates.

One thing here would have shocked Athens. The guardians hold no private property and no families, their children are raised in common, and the women of that class are educated and tested exactly as the men are and may rule. Plato also approves of controlling who breeds with whom, and of a founding myth he calls a noble falsehood.
ch.cap: Firelight, shadows and the long climb out
ch.h: The Cave, and the Climb Back Down

b: The eighth book is the part worth reading twice. Plato traces how constitutions rot, each into the next. Rule by the best decays into rule by the honour hungry, who prize winning and standing above wisdom. That decays into oligarchy, the rule of the rich, which breeds a resentful poor. Oligarchy falls to democracy, which he describes almost with affection as the most colourful of regimes, where every way of life is on display and nobody has to do anything in particular.

Democracy dies of its own best quality. Liberty becomes the only recognised good, every appetite gets called a right, and restraint begins to look like oppression. In the noise a champion of the people rises, takes the popular side against the rich, acquires a bodyguard, finds enemies the city needs protecting from, and becomes the tyrant. Freedom with no order does not stay free. It hands itself to a protector. In the ninth book that tyrant turns out to be the most wretched man alive, ruled by his worst part, friendless, suspicious, a prisoner inside his own power.

Then the real world asked for a demonstration. In 367 BC Dionysius the first died in Syracuse, and Dion wrote to Plato: the new ruler is young, come and make a philosopher of him. Plato was about sixty. He went. Dionysius the second enjoyed being taught by the famous Athenian and would not do the work, the court turned on tutor and friend alike, and within months Dion was exiled. Plato tried again in 361 and it went worse. He got out with help from Archytas.

Dion lost patience with philosophy and took Syracuse by force in 357 BC. Three years later his own associates murdered him. The man who argued all his life that only the wise should rule failed twice to improve one teachable prince, and watched his best pupil in politics become a conqueror and then a corpse.
ch.cap: Plato returns to Syracuse to school a young tyrant
ch.h: How a Free City Talks Itself Into a Tyrant
ch.when: In the dialogue, and Syracuse, 367 to 354 BC

b: The tenth book banishes the poets more firmly, on the grounds that imitation stands three removes from the truth and that drama trains us to enjoy in a theatre what we would be ashamed of at home. Then, having argued for nine books that justice pays within one life, Plato widens the stakes beyond it.

He finishes with a story. A soldier called Er is killed in battle, and twelve days later, lying on the funeral pyre, he wakes and tells what he saw. Souls arriving from a thousand years of reward or punishment come to a place where the lives of the next generation lie laid out on the ground, animal and human, famous and obscure, and each must choose one. Almost every soul chooses badly, out of habit, snatching at tyranny or wealth or beauty without looking at what comes attached.

The one who chooses well is Odysseus, who draws the last lot, takes his time, and picks the quiet life of a private man who minds his own business. Then they all drink from a river called Forgetfulness and are born. Your life, Plato is saying, is chosen by the character you have already built, whether or not you are paying attention.

Plato died in Athens at about eighty, in 348 or 347 BC, having run the Academy for forty years. In 1945 Karl Popper called The Republic the founding text of totalitarian politics, and he was not being frivolous: the censorship, the official lie and the managed breeding are all on the page. Others answer that the city is never offered as a plan, only as a city in words built to make one soul visible. What nobody disputes is the question it will not take back. Is it better for you, actually and not reputationally, to be a good person in a world where you could get away with not being one?
ch.cap: A soldier returns from the dead to describe the choosing

connects: Thucydides records the Athenian catastrophes Plato grew up inside, so the two books are the same decades seen once as history and once as philosophy.
Machiavelli answers Plato's question in reverse, asking what a ruler must actually do rather than what justice is, and the two books have been arguing with each other ever since.
Marcus Aurelius is the nearest thing history produced to Plato's philosopher ruler, and his private notebooks show what the job actually felt like from the inside.
note: Plato's dates and the Syracuse visits rest largely on the seventh letter attributed to him and on Diogenes Laertius, writing some five hundred years later, so they are firm in outline and soft in detail, and the letter's authenticity is still argued over. The tale of Plato being sold as a slave on Aegina, and the motto about geometry over the Academy door, are late traditions and are flagged as doubtful in the telling; the reported travels in Egypt and Cyrene are poorly evidenced. The summary of the dialogue follows the standard text of books one to ten. Karl Popper's charge in The Open Society and Its Enemies of 1945, that the book is a blueprint for totalitarianism, is given as the live criticism it remains.
recall: What does Thrasymachus claim justice is, and why does it force the rest of the book?

He claims justice is nothing but the advantage of the stronger: rules written by whoever holds power, in their own interest, and then taught to everyone else as morality. That reduces morality to a con played on the weak, so Plato has to show that justice benefits the person who has it, not only the person who imposes it.
What is the ring of Gyges, and whose challenge is it?

It is a ring of invisibility found by a shepherd, who uses it to seduce the queen, kill the king and take the kingdom. Glaucon, one of Plato's own brothers in the dialogue, uses it to ask whether anyone would stay just if they could never be caught. That is the question the remaining nine books answer.
What are the three parts of the soul, and what shows they are separate?

Reason, spirit and appetite. Plato argues that one thing cannot both want and refuse the same drink at the same moment, so a thirsty man who declines water must contain more than one part. The story of Leontius, desperate to look at corpses and disgusted with himself for wanting to, shows spirit set against appetite.
In the allegory of the cave, what happens after the prisoner gets out?

He is obliged to go back down. His eyes no longer work in the dark, he argues clumsily about shadows with men who never left, and Socrates says drily that they would kill him if they could. Plato wrote that about twenty five years after an Athenian jury executed Socrates.
What happened when Plato tried to put the theory into practice at Syracuse?

He sailed in 367 BC at Dion's invitation to educate the young Dionysius the second, and failed. A second attempt in 361 went worse and he was effectively detained. Dion later took Syracuse by force in 357 BC and was murdered by his own associates in 354.
recap: Plato was born in Athens at about 428 BC, into a governing family, in the middle of a war his city would lose. He grew up through the plague, the catastrophe in Sicily, the trial of Athens' own victorious generals, and the surrender of 404, when the long walls came down to the sound of flutes. Then thirty men, two of them his relatives, ran Athens for eight murderous months, and an old questioner named Socrates refused their order to help arrest an innocent man and simply went home. Four years later the restored democracy voted, lawfully and by a fair procedure, to kill that same old man. Plato was twenty eight, and the rest of his life is an answer to it. He went west, met the Pythagorean mathematician Archytas, and found in geometry a kind of truth no assembly could overturn. Back home, at around 387 BC, he founded the Academy in a grove outside the walls, where a teenage Aristotle would arrive in 367. Somewhere in the 370s he wrote The Republic. In it Thrasymachus says justice is nothing but the advantage of the stronger, and Glaucon sharpens it with the ring that makes you invisible: would anyone stay honest if they could never be caught? Plato's answer is to build a city in words so that justice becomes large enough to see, and then to find the same shape in a person. Justice is each part doing its own work, in a city and in a soul where reason governs, spirit enforces and appetite is fed but not obeyed. Injustice is civil war inside one head, which is why it damages you whether or not anyone finds out. Only those who love what is really the case should rule, he argues, and shows us prisoners watching shadows on a cave wall, with the one who escapes obliged to climb back down into the dark and be disbelieved. He then traces how a free city, making liberty its only good, talks itself into the arms of a protector who becomes a tyrant, and how that tyrant is the most wretched man alive. Twice, in 367 and 361 BC, he went to Syracuse to make a philosopher out of a real prince, and twice he failed. He died at about eighty, in 348 or 347 BC. Here is the line to remember. Injustice is not a crime that pays, it is a civil war inside the only place you can never leave.
stories: In 404 BC Sparta installed thirty men to run defeated Athens, and they set about killing wealthy residents for their estates. They summoned Socrates and ordered him to help arrest a rich man called Leon of Salamis. Socrates, who held no office and had no protection of any kind, listened to the order and then walked home. He explained at his own trial five years later that he was not afraid of the government, only of doing something unjust. The Thirty were finished within months. The democracy that replaced them executed him anyway.
Athens Puts Its Winners On Trial

In 406 BC an Athenian fleet beat the Spartans at Arginusae. A storm blew up afterwards and the generals failed to recover the men clinging to the wrecks. So Athens, having just won, tried its victorious commanders in the assembly and executed several of them. One of the presiding officials that day refused to put the illegal motion to a vote. His name was Socrates. Plato was in his twenties and watching. It is worth remembering whenever someone says he disliked democracy for snobbish reasons. He had seen it, in a good mood, kill the men who had just saved it.
The Tutor Sent to a Tyrant

In 367 BC the tyrant of Syracuse died, and his brother in law Dion wrote to Plato, then about sixty. The heir is young, come and make a philosopher of him. Plato sailed. Dionysius the second enjoyed being taught by the famous Athenian and would not do the work, the court turned on them both, and Dion was exiled within months. Plato went back in 361 and it went worse, and he got out with difficulty. Dion took the city by force in 357 and was murdered by his own friends in 354. The man who argued that only the wise should rule never managed to install one.
take: A majority can be lawful, sincere and completely wrong
Proper procedure is not proof of a right answer. Judge the decision and the process separately, and never let the fact that something was correctly approved stand in for whether it is correct.
Answer the strongest objection, not the weakest
Plato gave Thrasymachus and Glaucon the best version of his opponents' case before replying. Before any decision that matters, write down the sharpest argument against it in its own words.
Justice is each part doing its own work
Most dysfunction is one part reaching outside its job. Find the place where a single function in your life or business has quietly taken over decisions that belong to someone else.
The test of a value is what you do unobserved
Use the ring of Gyges as an audit. Any practice that only survives because nobody sees it is not a practice, it is an exposure waiting to be found.
Appetite is to be fed, not obeyed
You will not win by suppressing what you want. Set the policy while calm, in advance, then let the wanting arrive and do nothing about it.
Climbing out is only half the duty
Whoever understands something has to go back down and explain it badly to people who have not seen it. Expect that to be thankless and do it anyway.
Liberty with no restraint invites a protector
Watch any system that removes all friction at once. Ungoverned freedom tends to concentrate power in whoever offers to manage the resulting mess.
Character does the choosing before you arrive
By the time a big decision is in front of you, your habits have already narrowed the options. Build them now, deliberately, on small things nobody is watching.
title: The Man Whose City Killed His Teacher
wiifm: You will finish this knowing why one defeated Athenian decided that a crowd can be sincerely, lawfully and completely wrong, and what he built to answer it. You get the ring that makes you invisible, the three parts of a soul, the cave full of shadows, and the chain by which a free city talks itself into a tyrant, each arriving where he found it. You also get the awkward parts said out loud, the censorship and the noble lie, because the book is more useful honest than tidy. And you get his question, which is still yours. Is being good good for you when nobody is looking?
words: A way of getting at the truth by argument, in which a claim is tested by objection until what survives is better than what you started with.
Plato makes it the final stage of a guardian's training, years of having your own best arguments taken apart.
Rule by those who prize honour and public standing above everything else.
It is the first stage of decay in the eighth book, the regime that replaces rule by the wise.
A leader who gains power by rousing the feelings and resentments of ordinary people rather than by argument.
Plato's tyrant begins as exactly this, a champion of the people who then acquires a bodyguard.
The state of being genuinely stuck, where every answer you had has been shown not to work.
Socrates leaves Polemarchus and Thrasymachus there in the first book, and Plato is careful to show that it is not the same as an answer.
Imitation, the copying of something real by art or performance.
The tenth book banishes the poets on the grounds that imitation stands three removes from the truth.
